nodes.label: Ordinary Mathematical Induction
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in logic and proof methods (universal and existential quantifiers, direct proof, contradiction, counterexamples), standard algebra, and elementary sequence/summation notation (∑_{k=1}^n a_k). Establishes the Principle of Mathematical Induction on ℕ and shifted starting values n ≥ n₀: explicitly defining the predicate P(n), verifying the base case P(n₀), stating the inductive hypothesis P(k) for an arbitrary fixed k ≥ n₀ (confronting the circular misconception of assuming P(n) for all n), and proving the inductive step P(k) ⇒ P(k + 1). Trains ordinary induction across three distinct mathematical domains—summation identities (such as ∑ k² and finite geometric sums), divisibility claims (such as 3 | (4^n − 1)), and inequalities (such as 2^n > n² for n ≥ 5 and Bernoulli's inequality (1 + x)^n ≥ 1 + nx for x > −1)—so the learner does not conflate induction with summation formulas alone. Diagnoses classic broken induction proofs, including omitted base cases and hidden domain gaps in the inductive step (such as the k = 1 → k = 2 failure in the "all horses are the same color" fallacy). Enables the learner to formulate predicates cleanly and prove statements indexed by integers via weak induction. Leaves strong induction, well-ordering, and recursive structures to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Strong Induction and the Well-Ordering Principle
nodes.explanation: Builds on ordinary mathematical induction to develop strong (complete) induction and the Well-Ordering Principle (WOP) on ℕ. Formulates strong induction—assuming P(n₀), P(n₀ + 1), ..., P(k) to deduce P(k + 1)—and clarifies why multiple explicit base cases are often required when the inductive step looks back by a fixed lag (such as coin/postage-stamp representations n = 3a + 5b for n ≥ 8 or bounds on multi-step sequences like Fibonacci numbers) or splits an integer into arbitrary smaller factors (proving existence of prime factorization for all integers n ≥ 2). Introduces the Well-Ordering Principle (every nonempty subset of ℕ has a least element) and proves the logical equivalence of ordinary induction, strong induction, and WOP (defining Q(k) ≡ ∀j ≤ k, P(j) to derive strong from weak induction, and applying minimal-counterexample contradiction for WOP). Applies WOP directly to prove the integer division algorithm (existence of quotient and remainder) or minimal-counterexample results. Enables the learner to diagnose when weak induction stalls, choose the right number of base cases for strong induction, and translate smoothly between strong induction and minimal-counterexample proofs. Leaves structural induction on recursively generated objects to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Recursive Definitions and Structural Induction
nodes.explanation: Builds on strong induction and the Well-Ordering Principle to work with recursively defined sequences and discrete structures. Distinguishes recursive specifications (base values/objects plus constructor rules) from closed-form formulas, practicing verification of closed forms and bounds for multi-term recurrences (such as Fibonacci/Lucas identities and linear recurrence formulas supplied for verification, without developing general characteristic-equation or generating-function solvers). Introduces recursively defined discrete sets—such as full binary trees, balanced-parenthesis strings, arithmetic expression trees, and subsets of ℤ² generated from initial seeds—and develops structural induction: proving a property holds for every generated element by verifying all base objects and proving every constructor preserves the property (justifying soundness via strong induction on construction depth or object size). Applies structural induction to invariants such as leaves = internal nodes + 1 in full binary trees or equal left/right counts in balanced strings. Enables the learner to write unambiguous recursive definitions and prove global invariants of recursively constructed objects. Leaves combinatorial counting recurrences until counting tools are established.

nodes.label: Sum, Product, Complement, and Division Rules of Counting
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in logic and proof methods, elementary arithmetic, and informal finite-set notation (membership, subsets, union, intersection, disjointness, and size |A|). Establishes the four foundational finite-counting principles: the Addition (Sum) Rule for pairwise disjoint unions, the Multiplication (Product) Rule for multistage decisions (explicitly verifying that the number of choices at each stage is invariant across earlier choices, and splitting into additive cases whenever stage counts depend on prior picks), the Subtraction (Complement) Rule (|A| = |U| − |U \ A| for "at least one" constraints), and the Division Rule (dividing by k when a counting procedure generates every target configuration exactly k times). Introduces finite bijection counting—establishing |A| = |B| via a one-to-one correspondence—to derive the 2^n subsets of an n-element set (via length-n bitstrings) and the n^m functions from an m-element set to an n-element set. Targets the primary beginner errors of hidden overcounting, conflating disjoint unions with overlapping ones, and forcing dependent choices into a single product. Enables the learner to decompose elementary finite counting problems cleanly using sum, product, complement, division, and bijection arguments. Leaves permutations, combinations, pigeonhole arguments, and overlapping-union inclusion–exclusion to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: The Pigeonhole Principle and Generalized Pigeonhole Arguments
nodes.explanation: Builds on fundamental counting principles (and contradiction from assumed logic background) to prove non-constructive collision and existence results in finite combinatorics. Establishes the Simple Pigeonhole Principle (placing n + 1 objects into n boxes forces some box to hold at least two) and the Generalized Pigeonhole Principle (placing N objects into k boxes forces some box to contain at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects, proved by contradiction using the sum rule). Focuses on the central creative bridge—designing non-obvious "pigeons" and "pigeonholes"—across diverse worked uses: number theory (two integers with the same remainder mod n; choosing n + 1 numbers from {1, ..., 2n} always yields a pair where one divides the other, using odd-part factorization a = 2^r m as boxes; subset-sum collisions), plane geometry (five points in a 2 × 2 square yield a pair within distance √2), and finite networks (two people at a gathering have the same number of acquaintances). Clarifies that Pigeonhole proves existence without identifying which box overflows, and checks sharpness by exhibiting extremal configurations that narrowly avoid a collision. Enables the learner to formulate pigeonhole partitions and verify exact threshold counts. Leaves Ramsey-number extensions to an optional enrichment lesson.

nodes.label: Permutations and Ordered Arrangements
nodes.explanation: Builds on the product, complement, and division counting rules to count ordered selections and constrained arrangements. Introduces factorial notation n! (establishing 0! = 1 combinatorially as the single empty arrangement), derives k-permutations P(n, k) = n!/(n − k)! for ordered selections without repetition (interpreting them also as injective maps from a k-set to an n-set), and derives multiset permutations n!/(n₁! n₂! ··· n_r!) for arranging n objects with indistinguishable repeats via the division rule. Develops circular permutations ((n − 1)! for distinct objects up to rotation, contrasting necklace/reflection symmetry where dividing by 2 requires n ≥ 3) and standard constraint-modeling techniques: bundling required adjacent items into super-elements, applying the gap/insertion method for required non-adjacent items, and using complement counting for forbidden adjacencies. Enables the learner to count ordered arrangements with repetition, circular symmetry, and adjacency constraints without overcounting. Leaves unordered subsets, binomial coefficients, and combinations with repetition to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Combinations, Binomial Coefficients, and Combinatorial Proofs
nodes.explanation: Builds on permutations and ordered arrangements to count unordered selections without repetition and introduce combinatorial proof by double counting. Derives the binomial coefficient C(n, k) = P(n, k)/k! = n!/(k!(n − k)!) via the division rule (setting C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1 and C(n, k) = 0 for k < 0 or k > n) and develops its three core interpretations: k-element subsets of an n-set, length-n bitstrings with weight k, and northeast lattice paths from (0, 0) to (k, n − k). Trains combinatorial double-counting proofs—counting one clearly defined finite set in two independent ways—to establish symmetry C(n, k) = C(n, n − k), Pascal's identity C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k), the committee-chair identity k C(n, k) = n C(n − 1, k − 1), the hockey-stick identity, and Vandermonde's identity ∑ C(m, k)C(n, r − k) = C(m + n, r). Directly diagnoses the classic overcounting trap in "at least one / at least k" committee selections (picking required representatives first and then "any remaining" members counts multi-representative committees multiple times). Enables the learner to count unordered configurations accurately and write rigorous combinatorial proofs of binomial identities. Leaves the Binomial Theorem and selections with repetition to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Combinations with Repetition, Stars and Bars, and Compositions
nodes.explanation: Builds on combinations and binomial coefficients to count unordered selections with repetition and nonnegative/positive integer compositions. Proves the stars-and-bars bijection between k-element multisets chosen from n types (equivalently nonnegative integer solutions to x₁ + x₂ + ··· + x_n = k) and binary strings of k stars and n − 1 bars, yielding C(k + n − 1, n − 1) = C(k + n − 1, k), and adapts it to positive integer solutions (strong compositions, x_i ≥ 1) yielding C(k − 1, n − 1). Develops constraint transformations: handling lower bounds x_i ≥ a_i via the variable shift y_i = x_i − a_i and handling inequality sums x₁ + ··· + x_n ≤ k via a nonnegative slack variable x_{n+1}, while explicitly noting that upper-bound constraints x_i ≤ b_i cannot be handled by shifting alone and motivate inclusion–exclusion. Synthesizes the four elementary selection regimes (ordered vs. unordered crossed with repetition allowed vs. forbidden: n^k, P(n, k), C(k + n − 1, k), C(n, k)) so the learner can distinguish them reliably from problem descriptions. Enables the learner to solve multiset and lower-bounded integer-equation counting problems cleanly. Leaves upper-bounded integer solutions to inclusion–exclusion.

nodes.label: The Binomial and Multinomial Theorems
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes ordinary mathematical induction with combinations and Pascal's identity to establish algebraic expansions of powers and their combinatorial consequences. Proves the Binomial Theorem (x + y)^n = ∑_{k=0}^n C(n, k) x^{n−k} y^k in two complementary ways—combinatorially (selecting which k of the n factors contribute y) and rigorously by ordinary induction on n using Pascal's identity—so the learner connects algebraic manipulation with counting arguments. Extracts core identities by substituting values into (1 + x)^n (yielding ∑ C(n, k) = 2^n, the alternating sum ∑ (−1)^k C(n, k) = 0 for n ≥ 1, and equal counts of even- and odd-sized subsets) and via elementary algebraic/combinatorial coefficient extraction (such as ∑ k C(n, k) = n 2^{n−1}). Generalizes to the Multinomial Theorem (x₁ + ··· + x_r)^n = ∑ C(n; k₁, ..., k_r) x₁^{k₁} ··· x_r^{k_r} using multiset permutations from earlier ancestors to extract specific polynomial coefficients. Enables the learner to expand powers, compute exact coefficients, and deploy the alternating binomial identity as a proof engine. Leaves the Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion (which uses the alternating sum crucially) to the next lesson.

nodes.label: The Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion
nodes.explanation: Builds on the Binomial Theorem (specifically the alternating binomial-sum identity ∑_{k=0}^m (−1)^k C(m, k) = 0 for m ≥ 1, along with induction and basic counting rules from earlier ancestors) to count unions and complements of overlapping finite sets when the addition rule breaks down. Motivates the alternating-sign correction through 2-set and 3-set overlapping Venn problems, then formulates both equivalent forms of the general n-set Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion: the union formula |⋃_{i=1}^n A_i| and the complement formula |⋂_{i=1}^n A_i^c| = |U| − ∑ |A_i| + ∑ |A_i ∩ A_j| − ··· + (−1)^n |⋂ A_i|. Proves the general theorem via element-contribution counting (an element in exactly m ≥ 1 sets contributes ∑_{k=0}^m (−1)^k C(m, k) = 0 to the complement formula, whereas an element in 0 sets contributes 1) and notes how an inductive proof on n yields the same identity. Applies PIE to foundational problems—counting integers in {1, ..., N} not divisible by given primes (deriving Euler's totient formula φ(n) for concrete prime factorizations) and counting bitstrings or permutations avoiding several forbidden substrings. Enables the learner to set up property sets A_i, compute intersection sizes cleanly, and prove and apply PIE. Leaves derangements, surjections, and upper-bounded compositions to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Derangements, Surjections, and Bounded Compositions via Inclusion–Exclusion
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes stars-and-bars compositions with the Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion to solve three flagship university counting problems where designing the universe U and forbidden properties A_i requires genuine modeling. First, counts nonnegative integer solutions to x₁ + ··· + x_n = k subject to upper bounds x_i ≤ b_i by defining A_i as the violation x_i ≥ b_i + 1 and computing each intersection size via shifted stars and bars. Second, counts surjective (onto) functions from an m-element set onto an n-element set (defining surjectivity locally as every target element being hit at least once) by forbidding omitted codomain elements, deriving surj(m, n) = ∑_{j=0}^n (−1)^j C(n, j)(n − j)^m and introducing Stirling numbers of the second kind S(m, n) = surj(m, n)/n! for partitioning m labeled items into n nonempty unlabeled blocks. Third, counts derangements D_n (permutations with no fixed points) by setting A_i = {σ : σ(i) = i}, proving D_n = n! ∑_{k=0}^n (−1)^k/k! and noting how D_n/n! rapidly approaches 1/e (connecting to the Maclaurin series of e^{−1} as a brief interpretive remark). Enables the learner to solve bounded-composition, surjection, set-partition, and derangement problems end to end via PIE.

nodes.label: Setting Up and Proving Combinatorial Recurrences
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes recursive definitions and structural/strong induction with combinations and combinatorial proofs to model counting problems recursively and prove closed forms or identities about the resulting sequences. Trains the combinatorial decomposition technique—partitioning the set of size-n configurations by the first or last piece, symbol, or block—to derive recurrence relations and exact initial conditions for classical families: binary strings avoiding "11" (Fibonacci recurrence), 2 × n domino tilings, ternary strings with parity constraints, subset/composition counts, the triangular recurrence S(m, n) = S(m − 1, n − 1) + n S(m − 1, n) for partitions of an m-set into n nonempty blocks, and the combinatorial derangement recurrence D_n = (n − 1)(D_{n−1} + D_{n−2}) obtained directly by analyzing where element 1 maps. Uses ordinary and strong induction to prove conjectured closed forms, explicit bounds, and combinatorial identities (such as Cassini's identity or D_n = n D_{n−1} + (−1)^n) directly from the recurrences. Enables the learner to translate discrete counting problems into valid recurrences with accurate base cases and verify closed-form solutions rigorously, leaving systematic recurrence-solving machinery (characteristic equations and generating functions) to a subsequent discrete-mathematics module.

nodes.label: Elementary Ramsey Theory via Generalized Pigeonhole
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing the Pigeonhole Principle with the Binomial Theorem (using ordinary mathematical induction and Pascal's identity established in earlier ancestors) to introduce finite Ramsey theory. Defines the two-color Ramsey number R(s, t) as the smallest integer N such that any red/blue coloring of pairs among N vertices contains a red s-clique or a blue t-clique, establishes trivial values R(s, 2) = s and R(2, t) = t, and proves R(3, 3) = 6 (the party problem) in full: upper bound via generalized Pigeonhole on the 5 edges incident to a chosen vertex, and lower bound R(3, 3) > 5 via an explicit 2-coloring of the 5-cycle without monochromatic triangles. Proves the Erdős–Szekeres recurrence inequality R(s, t) ≤ R(s − 1, t) + R(s, t − 1) (with strict improvement when both terms are even, yielding R(3, 4) ≤ 9) via generalized Pigeonhole on a single vertex's neighborhood, and deduces the finite upper bound R(s, t) ≤ C(s + t − 2, s − 1) by ordinary induction on m = s + t using Pascal's identity. Enables the learner to prove small Ramsey bounds and construct explicit lower-bound colorings, leaving probabilistic lower bounds and infinite Ramsey theory to later combinatorics.

nodes.label: Synthesizing Counting Models: Balls, Boxes, and the Twelvefold Way
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing derangements/surjections/bounded compositions with combinatorial recurrences to organize elementary counting into Rota's Twelvefold Way. Classifies distribution problems of placing m balls into n boxes—equivalently counting functions f : M → N—across three independent axes: balls labeled vs. unlabeled, boxes labeled vs. unlabeled, and restriction type (arbitrary, injective / at most one per box, or surjective / at least one per box). Consolidates all previously established formulas into one coherent decision matrix: n^m, P(n, m), surj(m, n) = n! S(m, n), C(m + n − 1, m), C(n, m), C(m − 1, n − 1), Stirling numbers S(m, n), and sums of Stirling numbers (Bell numbers), while identifying the remaining unlabeled-balls/unlabeled-boxes cells as integer partitions p(m, n) and explaining why they require recurrences or generating functions rather than elementary closed forms. Trains rapid model identification on disguised word problems by determining distinguishability and occupancy constraints before selecting a formula.
